items.followUp: Describe the role of the small intestine in human digestion.

rubric.why: Award for identifying the stomach’s storage role.
rubric.how: State that food is held in the stomach before passing onward.

rubric.why: Award for describing mechanical digestion in the stomach.
rubric.description: Muscular contractions churn and mix food with gastric juice.
rubric.how: Mention both churning/mixing and gastric juice.

rubric.why: Award for the key components of gastric juice and their roles.
rubric.description: Hydrochloric acid provides an acidic medium and pepsin digests proteins.
rubric.how: Name HCl and pepsin, and state their relevant roles.

rubric.why: Award for a further stomach function stated in the answer.
rubric.description: Mucus protects the stomach lining, and the partly digested food passes as chyme to the small intestine.
rubric.how: Name either protection by mucus or the passage of chyme to the small intestine.

modelAnswer: The stomach is a muscular, J-shaped sac that temporarily stores food.
Its muscular walls churn and mix food with gastric juice.
Hydrochloric acid in gastric juice provides an acidic medium, while pepsin begins the digestion of proteins.
Mucus protects the stomach lining; the partly digested food, called chyme, then passes into the small intestine.

items.followUp: Define population and state its two types.

rubric.why: Award for the defining features of a community.
rubric.description: A community consists of populations of different species living in the same area or habitat.
rubric.how: Include different species/populations and a shared area or habitat.

rubric.why: Award for naming the two types of community.
rubric.description: The two types are major communities and minor communities.

modelAnswer: A community is all the populations of different species living and interacting in the same area or habitat.
Communities are of two types: major communities and minor communities.

items.followUp: What is the unicellular type of cellular organization? Give one example.

rubric.why: Award for describing the arrangement of cells in a colony.
rubric.description: In colonial organization, similar cells live together in a group or colony.
rubric.how: State that cells are grouped together as a colony.

rubric.why: Award for explaining cell independence or giving the standard example.
rubric.description: The cells can carry out life functions independently; Volvox is an example.
rubric.how: Mention independent functioning or name Volvox.

modelAnswer: In colonial cellular organization, similar cells live together in a group called a colony.
The cells can perform life functions independently; Volvox is an example.

rubric.why: Award for the correct subject of Cell Biology.
rubric.description: Cell Biology is the study of cells.
rubric.how: Define Cell Biology by stating that it studies cells.

rubric.why: Award for the correct subject of Histology.
rubric.description: Histology is the study of tissues.
rubric.how: Define Histology by stating that it studies tissues.

modelAnswer: Cell Biology is the branch of biology that studies cells.
Histology is the branch of biology that studies tissues.

items.followUp: What is a conclusion in the biological method?

rubric.why: Award for explaining that experimental results are brought together.
rubric.description: Summarization means organizing and presenting the results of an investigation concisely.
rubric.how: Refer to summarizing or organizing the results.

rubric.why: Award for connecting the summarized results to the outcome of the investigation.
rubric.description: The summary is used to draw a conclusion about whether the hypothesis is supported or rejected.
rubric.how: State that the results lead to a conclusion about the hypothesis.

modelAnswer: Summarization of results means organizing and presenting the results of an investigation in a concise form.
The summarized results are used to draw a conclusion about whether the hypothesis is supported or rejected.

items.followUp: Give one example each of a quantitative and a qualitative observation.

rubric.why: Award for identifying the measurable, numerical nature of quantitative observations.
rubric.description: Quantitative observations are expressed as numbers or measurements.
rubric.how: State that they are numerical or measurable.

rubric.why: Award for a valid advantage over qualitative observations.
rubric.description: They are more objective and precise, and are easier to compare and analyze.
rubric.how: Give at least one valid reason why quantitative observations are better.

modelAnswer: Quantitative observations are expressed as numbers or measurements.
They are generally more objective and precise than qualitative observations, and are easier to compare and analyze.

items.followUp: State one function of the middle lamella in plant cells.

rubric.why: Award for a correct feature of the primary wall.
rubric.description: The primary wall is formed first and is thin and flexible while the cell grows.
rubric.how: State when it forms or describe it as thin/flexible during growth.

rubric.why: Award for a correct contrasting feature of the secondary wall.
rubric.description: The secondary wall forms inside the primary wall after cell growth and is generally thicker.
rubric.how: State its position, time of formation, or greater thickness.

modelAnswer: The primary wall is the first wall formed; it is thin and flexible, allowing the growing cell to expand.
The secondary wall is deposited inside the primary wall after the cell has stopped growing and is generally thicker.

items.followUp: What is osmosis, and does it require cellular energy?

rubric.why: Award for stating that passive transport does not use cellular energy.
rubric.description: Passive transport does not require cellular energy.
rubric.how: State that no energy or ATP is required.

rubric.why: Award for stating the direction of passive transport.
rubric.description: Substances move down their concentration gradient, from higher to lower concentration.
rubric.how: Describe movement down the gradient or from high to low concentration.

modelAnswer: Passive transport moves substances down their concentration gradient, from higher to lower concentration, without using cellular energy.
Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient, from lower to higher concentration, and requires energy, usually ATP.
